title: In secret
hookLine: if you live simply or drink only water, don't announce it (Enchiridion 47)

lines: DAY FOUR OF A NEW HABIT.
cards: Day four of a new habit. No sugar, or a cold shower every morning, or a run at six. And there it is, the itch to mention it.
A casual line at lunch: oh, I don't eat sugar anymore. A photo of the sunrise from mile two. For a lot of people, half the pleasure of a discipline is others knowing about it.
Epictetus saw this itch in his students, and in section forty-seven he names it, with a picture of a well-known philosopher hugging a frozen statue.

teach.b: Once you've trained your body to live simply, Epictetus says, don't preen about it. If you drink only water, don't announce at every chance: I drink water.
If you want to train yourself for hardship, do it for yourself, not for those outside. Don't go hugging statues. That's a jab at an old story.
Diogenes the Cynic, the ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says, used to embrace statues covered in snow in winter, to toughen himself.
Epictetus admired Diogenes deeply, but he knew how easily a hard practice becomes a public performance.

teach.h: SPIT OUT THE WATER. TELL NO ONE.
teach.b: His alternative: when you're very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. A small, private test that nobody sees, and those last three words are the whole practice.

teach.h: ANNOUNCED, IT WORKS FOR THE AUDIENCE.
teach.b: A discipline you announce starts working for the audience. You get the reward early, in other people's admiration, and the habit quietly changes its purpose.
A discipline you keep secret has only one job: to change you. A neighbor tradition says something close.
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about giving to the poor in the King James words: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth."
Two teachers, two different reasons, each in its own house, and a shared picture: some good things grow best in the dark, like roots.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism keep their personal disciplines private, so the practice serves their own growth rather than other people's admiration.

o: hiding what you do because you're ashamed of it
keeping a discipline to yourself so it changes you
keeping other people's private news to yourself

p: spit it out, tell no one

s: he says train for yourself, not for those outside.
the snowy statue story is told about Diogenes the Cynic
the ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says he embraced snow-covered statues to toughen himself.
Epictetus says to announce a discipline so friends keep you accountable
his practice ends with tell no one.

games.q: a month without sugar, and someone at lunch offers cake. what fits Enchiridion 47?
o: explain your no-sugar journey in detail.
a simple no, thanks, and change the subject.
eat it to avoid making a scene.
games.why: don't preen. if you drink water, don't say at every chance: I drink water. the discipline is for you.

practice: Think of one discipline you keep, or would like to: a walk, a fast, a kindness, a limit on your phone, a habit of prayer or quiet. Ask yourself honestly who knows about it, and whether you want them to.
Then picture keeping it entirely to yourself, even when there's an opening to mention it.

wordCard.voice: In secret. Enchiridion forty-seven: train for yourself, not for those outside. Spit out the cold water, and tell no one. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: tell no one. Some of the best work is never seen. Until tomorrow.
